utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 22nd of July 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us today. Very briefly, some housekeeping matters. First of all, if there are any objections from anyone, we shall hold our hearing tomorrow morning and not tomorrow afternoon, because the courtroom is now free. Therefore, we will be able to sit tomorrow morning. That's the first point. Second point: This morning I signed an order pertaining to the fact that Wednesday, the 3rd of September at quarter past 2.00, we will have our hearing to try Mr. Petkovic. I would therefore like to ask the Prosecution to check its witnesses who will come as part of Mr. Seselj's trial, make sure they have a witness for Tuesday and another witness for the Thursday, because on Wednesday we shall be hearing Petkovic's case. That was the second announcement I had to make. The third is an oral decision which I wish to hand down now. It's a fairly short one which relates to the witness called Osman Kadic. Oral decision on the motion filed by the Prosecution on Osman Kadic pursuant to Rule 94 bis. Considering the statement made by the witness in question on the 12th of July, 2006, in light to 94 bis, requesting the statement and the documents that go with it; in light of document 262 that was filed by the Prosecution on the 29th of March, 2007, Mr. Seselj declared he was against these documents and challenged them, and reckoned that Mr. Osman Kadic was not an expert witness, and stipulated that he wished to cross-examine this witness, in light of the fact that these documents have been disclosed to the accused in a language he understands and in hard copy, on the 21st of September, 2007, pursuant to the Pre-Trial Judge's decision on the 9th of July, 2007. Considering the document 233 provided by the accused, dated the 2nd of November, 2007, in which the accused, first of all, challenges the fact that the documents disclosed are, in fact, an expert report, and therefore does not notify the Chamber pursuant to Rule 94 bis. Second point: He also states that he does challenge these documents and does not wish them to be presented. He wishes to cross-examine the witness himself, only after having received the proper expert report and the documents that go with it. Considering that in its previous decision relating to expert witnesses that I heard before the Chamber, this is how the Trial Chamber provides the definition of an expert witness: A person who, thanks to his or her knowledge, qualifications, or special qualification, can help a trier of fact understand or determine a legal issue, has also stated that the Trial Chamber addresses the curriculum vitae, article, publications, professional experience. I'm going too fast. Let me resume. Let me provide the definition of an expert. Let me read it out, slowly. Let me continue reading out this definition, as of line 22 ... or to determine a contentious issue. The Trial Chamber stated that it would bear in mind the curriculum vitae, the articles and publications and professional experience, or any other information relating to the said witness for which expert qualification is required. Considering that in light of the documents provided by the Prosecution, this witness was a doctor working in the Emergency Ward, but had no specific knowledge as far as forensic medicine was concerned. This person, therefore, has never conducted any other examinations or exhumations or postmortem examinations, other than the exhumation in Mostar, stated in his statement. For the foregoing reasons, the Trial Chamber dismisses the Prosecution's motion to admit these documents pursuant to Rule 94 bis and decides to hear the witness, Osman Kadic, as a witness of fact relating to the exhumations that were conducted in the Duborak [phoen] dump in Mostar. This witness will therefore be called as a simple mere witness and not an expert witness, pursuant to Rule 94 bis. A fourth point, which shall be a very short one: Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has noticed, on reading an e-mail sent by one of your associates, Mr. Krasic, that insulting words had been expressed vis a vis a representative of the Registry. We do not understand why your main associate thus insults the civil servants of the Registry. Had you been made aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you have to tell me what kind of message was involved and who the message was sent to. To whom did Zoran Krasic send a message, and then let's hear what's so insulting in the message. I really don't know what you're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this message has not been conveyed to you, we shall give it to you in the course of the afternoon. Then you will be able to see what is in this message. There is no point in addressing this any further. Whatever the case may be, we have material proof of the fact that there is an insult in this e-mail. As you know, this has created some friction. You are quite right, we need to disclose this document to you so you can see how you can reply to it, and if need be, you may tell us what you will do in the future to avoid this happening again. We have a witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, could you tell me who was the e-mail sent to? You can tell me that at least now. Is it an e-mail that Zoran Krasic sent to the Registry, because I'm not aware of him having sent e-mails to the Registry as of late at all; and I don't know what the reason would be for him to send e-mails to the Secretariat. As for e-mails to the Secretariat, it was only Marina Raguz, case manager who sent them, and that was the mail that was used for sending photographs and videos twice. Zoran Krasic does not have any communication whatsoever with the Registry. As for scheduling visits of legal advisers, all of that is handled by Marina Ragus as well, so I really doubt that Zoran Krasic sent an e-mail to the Registry at all. Let me tell you that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This e-mail which has been sent electronically will be disclosed to you. I don't have it at hand at the moment, but we will make sure that you receive it. Mr. Seselj, as you know, we have a 92 bis witness this afternoon. From what I understood, this witness did not wish to be granted any protective measures, but I need to make sure. Therefore, we shall move into closed session for the time being, and I will put the question to him. If he confirms that he does not wish to have such measures, we shall then lift the blinds. We shall drop the blinds for the moment and move into closed session. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had something to say to you before the witness walks into the courtroom. So should I wait for this music to stop, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I speak straight away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Let's move into closed session. I don't see the little logo on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you should oil the blinds a little bit. That means it would make less noise. Witness, could you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ibrahim Kujan from Nevesinje. I was born on the 21st of April, 1941. I'm from Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm involved in agriculture and politics; agriculture because I am an agricultural engineer and producer, and I'm in politics because I am a member of the Club of Bosniaks in the Parliament of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you're an elected official, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question before you make the solemn declaration: Have you already testified before a court of law on the events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is the first time that you testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few informative matters. We are under the 92 ter procedure of the Rules. This procedure will be conducted in this manner: The Prosecutor will first read a brief summary of your written statement. She will then put some questions to you. She may also show you a certain number of documents, and for your deposition we have -- actually, for that particular phase we have 30 minutes. The Judges may also put questions to you after this. The accused, who could have cross-examined you, but told us that he will not cross-examine you since he does not wish to put questions because we are proceeding under Rule 92 bis, so he did mention this on a couple of occasions. So Mr. Seselj will not put questions to you. So this is how the hearing will be held. It will be a short hearing, since the procedure has it that the Prosecutor has 30 minutes for you, and she will put a few questions to you. So, Ms. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you prefer that I read the a summary of Mr. Kujan's statement before authenticating it or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, actually, read it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Kujan is a Bosnian inhabitant from Nevesinje municipality. In 1991, at the beginning of the conflict, he was 30 years old. In June of 1991, a military unit called Karadjordje was set up in Nevesinje. The commander of this unit was Arsen Grahovac. The headquarters of the Karadjordje unit was a coffee bar called Ravna Gora. Members of the Karadjordje unit cooperated with the local police. However, they created roadblocks on all roads leading into Nevesinje, and they physically abused non-Serb people, whom they stopped at the barricades. In the Karadjordje unit were Chetniks who manned the check-points. They did not have to pay for their consumptions in certain bars and restaurants. The commander, Krsto Savic, provided refreshments, ammunition, food and money to the unit. Later, members of the Karadjordje unit started blowing up religious buildings and property belonging to Muslims in Nevesinje. Despite reporting these events to the police, there were no consequences visited upon the perpetrators. The war in Croatia started in the second half of 1991, and there was a general call for mobilisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. People in Nevesinje, Muslims and Croats in Nevesinje, were fired from their jobs. Their apartments were taken by force, and they were evicted without cause. Non-Serb members of the reserve police were not mobilised, and their posts were taken by ethnic Serbs. On 19 September 1991, JNA corps, including the Uzice Corps from Serbia arrived in Nevesinje. Among them were many JNA reserve soldiers who brought a large quantity of military equipment, including tanks, APCs, artillery weapons, and they took complete control of the area from Mostar and Trebinje. Their infantry never stopped shooting with their weapons, including anti-aircraft guns. They fired their weapons above the houses of Bosniaks. For those who were not ethnically Serb, life in Nevesinje became like a prison camp. The commander of the Uzice Corps was General Milan Torbice. On 22 September 1991, he organised a meeting of well-known and important Serbs in the municipality. The general gave a speech on that occasion saying that for Serbs the moment had arrived to fulfill their historic wishes, and that access to the sea and the border along the Osijek-Karlovac-Karlobag line could be achieved within weeks. After that speech, Mr. Kujan observed Serbs carrying automatic rifles, threatening non-Serbs in the streets with their weapons. They told non-Serbs that it was Serbian territory and they should leave. They plundered public property and took it back to Serbia. Non-Serbs were not permitted to withdraw savings from banks. Some people fled Nevesinje. An ethnic Serb Crisis Staff was established in the beginning of 1992, which took over control of the municipality and replaced the Municipal Assembly. Members of the Crisis Staff included the chief of the police, Mr. Savic, and Momcilo Golijanin, a deputy of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had direct connections to Radovan Karadzic. In April 1992, a few days before the shelling of Mostar began, large convoys of ethnic Serbs from Mostar began to arrive in Nevesinje. Leaders of SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Ms. Dahl. A summary is a summary. You know, if you give us a summary that's, in fact, a novel, then that's not really the idea. When you draft a summary, you have to focus on very important and meaningful moments, points.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm nearly finished. Refugees arrived and took the apartments of non-Serbs. In April 1992, there was an arrest campaign. Mr. Kujan and others fled to the woods. Serb forces attacked on 14 and 16 June. They attacked the southern part of the municipality. On 18 June, Mr. Kujan heard heavy explosions coming from the Gacko municipality. The attacks continued. They were directed by the local Serb police, members of the Karadjordje unit, Chetniks from Serbia and Montenegro, Arkan's men and Seselj's men, as well as regular army units. Mr. Kujan saw these attacks from a distant hill by using his binoculars. He saw troops wearing red berets as well as wearing White Eagle insignia. During these attacks, Serb troops killed elderly people who had remained behind in their homes. After the attack on Postoljani, Mr. Kujan and other members of the group he was with who had fled into the woods walked in the direction of Bjelimici in the Konjac municipality. Several elderly people who remained behind were later killed when they were trying to get food. When Mr. Kujan arrived in the Konjac municipality, he joined the Territorial Defence. In that position, he was allowed to interview Serbian prisoners who told him that all of the remaining non-Serbs in Nevesinje had been killed. Mr. Kujan has since compiled lists of the killed and missing. He can establish that 316 Muslims and Croats were killed, including 32 children under the age of 14. Later, he learned that on 26th June 1992, 72 persons were caught while trying to escape through the mountains and woods. They were captured on the Velez Mountain near a radio and TV installation. All but three were caught and killed. I'd ask the Registrar to bring up 65 ter number 5036.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Kujan, do you have your written statement dated 8 October 1998? If it's easier for you, it's also on the screen.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I have here all the necessary documentation, everything I need, and I would like to address the Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have to answer the questions that the Prosecutor will put to you. She will show you documents that you signed. That's the purpose of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Which documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me first ask you to take a look at the screen. The screen in front of you has your witness statement on it. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look at the statement. Is this your written statement that you gave on 8 October 1998?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: All that I signed is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does your signature appear at the bottom of the pages of the document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at the second part of your written statement dated 12 June 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, in the oral decision that we have rendered on the 9th of June, 2008, we had confirmed our decision of 27 February 2008, according to which this witness would be heard under Rule 92 ter regarding the statement that he gave on the 8th of October, 1998. That's all, and this is the statement that we have on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In our motion, we'd indicated that the statement signed in 2004 has a number of corrections in it that are an integral part of the first statement, and I can present those corrections orally or, for the interests of time, simply append that information to the original statement. I appreciate the distinction the Chamber is drawing, but I want to make sure that you have the most accurate and complete information available.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you provide the information contained in the written statement that is 65 ter Exhibit 5036?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I did make some corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we met, I asked you to review both statements to make sure they were correct, and you gave me some handwritten corrections that I've distributed previously to Mr. Seselj and to the Chamber. Can you go through the corrections with me, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Under item 7, where it says "summer 1991," where I refer to Vojislav Seselj, it was in fact the beginning of 1992. I can't remember the month or the date when he was in Nevesinje. I don't actually know Seselj. I had seen him once in the 1970s, and on that occasion when he was wearing a military uniform, when he came to Nevesinje with Bozidar Vucurevic, Arsen Grahovac and Mr. Sprema, and I didn't really care who he was with. That was the beginning of 1992, on the eve of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It could have been February or March. I can't remember the date. And on that occasion, Seselj was staying at Ravna Gora, which was a tavern and the basic of the Karadjordje Detachment. The information was given me by Erhan Djubor [phoen] and his driver.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat? He was saying this too quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What they were talking about, I don't know, and I don't really care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the name of the chauffeur? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tale Campara, and the information was given me by Erhan Djubor. There's another mistake. Instead of --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Just a second. I have your original annotations, and let's have them put on the ELMO so that the Chamber is able to follow along. For the record, the first correction that you referred to was at paragraph 7 with ERN number 0363-1644, e-court page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's very good, it's legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Kujan, would you proceed to the next correction that you made to your statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Instead of "Zejna Pijovic," it should be "Zejna Pajevic."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is on page 9 in e-court with the evidence registration number 036317.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Paragraph 17 of the document. Could Madam Registrar display that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the screen, sir, because the annotations are on the screen, and you have the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, you made a correction regarding when the mosques and church in Nevesinje were destroyed. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: The mosque was not destroyed, as it was written. All the mosques were destroyed later. An organised and professional team did that. They were quite qualified to handle explosives.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were they destroyed after --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Probably explosive experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: The mosques were all destroyed after Nevesinje was captured, and the Catholic Church and the two town mosques were completely blown away. Not even the foundations stayed intact. The stones are now being sorted to see what belongs to what, because all these buildings were listed as cultural heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were there any churches that were left standing in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbian church and some smaller Christian orthodox churches were left intact. The Catholic churches and mosques were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, please, to turn to the statement that you gave in 1998. And you included an additional name. It's at e-court page 15, and the evidence registration number on the top of the document is 03631653.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: It's very poorly legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you look on the screen again? They've got the device to show the picture.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I can see that now, yes, I can see very well. Since I was the commander of the reserve police force in Pridvorci, the mobilisation of police reservists at that time avoided Bosniaks. Bosniaks were not called up because weapons were being distributed and because the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was respected. Djuro Miseljic, not Djuro Radic replaced me. That's another correction I have to make here, as a newly mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you to turn to the page in e-court, page 17. It's 0363-1655, and you included the full name of Mr. Parezanin. Can you confirm that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Parezanin. I knew that a someone who was searching and interrogating some heads of families and setting ultimatums, we got an ultimatum on the 18th of May to turn over the weapons that we didn't have, and radio transmitters and all the rest, but this military security service used some methods that were worthy of Goebel in the Second World War. This man, whose last name was Parezanin, was called Svetozar. As far as I managed to learn, he was head of the Military Security Service. Nothing could be done without him. All the other units, including Seselj's men who were there, worked under his command. The people who actually went to negotiate with Svetozar Parezanin were given certain conditions. One of the conditions was for us to surrender, to turn over the people whom Svetozar thought to be extremist, including me, and to respond to the mobilisation call-up. And before the coup d'etat, the [indiscernible] in Nevesinje while Vuk Draskovic had power in Nevesinje, mobilisation worked very poorly. But after Radovan Karadzic and his party, the SDS, won the majority in the Parliament and in the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were impotent to do anything. And sometime in November/December 1991, these people were replaced, because practically they were not able to work any longer, because the brandishing of weapons above their heads was not really encouraging. I have to say in this procedure that I was the representative of Bosniaks in Nevesinje, where around 10 per cent of the population were killed, which is equal to Srebrenica's massacre, and I felt it was my moral duty to respond to the call of this Court, because there can be no justice without truth. I want to be absolutely fair, not to add anything or hold back anything. I'm not here to score points for any side, and I wanted this to be a public hearing so that everyone could hear. I'm saying again I saw Seselj once in passing in the 1980s in Sarajevo. I saw him in the beginning of 1992 in Nevesinje. And after that, I heard no more of him. But I heard that his people in Nevesinje were searching for Muslims, and there were cases when in some houses the refugees took over, Seselj's men came and said they were looking for Muslims. We said there were no Muslims. The massacre in Nevesinje happened after the withdrawal of Serbs from Mostar, Konjac and that region. That's from the 14th to the 28th of June. The people who remained in Nevesinje later ended up in prison or in third countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Dahl, you have five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Kujan, could you look at the last page of your statement below -- with the number of persons who were killed in Nevesinje, and you made some corrections. This is on the same page that we were on, but just at the bottom. It's --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I think we need to go one more. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Have you participated in the gathering of information about people who were killed or missing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I was the leader of the Displaced Persons of Nevesinje, that is, Bosniaks and Croats, people displaced during the last war. We gathered all the information. I have lists, if somebody wants to see them. We have a total of 350 civilians listed as missing of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity. However, later on some people reappeared, who managed to survive in the woods. One woman, with four children, managed to survive with the help of the Red Cross in Trebinje, so the number came down to 301 Bosniaks and Croats. Out of this number, 158 Bosniaks and 7 Croats were found dead, and we are still looking for another 148 Bosniaks and 8 Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With the permission of the Chamber, Mr. Kujan can speak to annex 10 of the third amended indictment, which is the schedule of victims whose remains are -- whose names are listed, and I'd like to have him review the list. I have copies for the Court. I had not anticipated, when I prepared the Court binder, that he would be able to review the list and testify as to its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I know, this is part of the civilians who had been killed. The group consisted of 72 missing civilians. These civilians were captured on mount Velez in Jasenov Do. Part of them were taken to the Alatnica in Nevesinje. Later on, according to my information, these missing civilians were killed near Lipovaca. In 1994, they were moved out of that pit, Lipovaca. We did not find out where the bones, the remains of these people are. Could you please -- could you show me the other part of the list now? Well, at any rate, it has to do with civilians from Knunapresik [phoen], the municipality of Nevesinje, and another village. It has to do with entire families, practically, from newborn babies to old men. So not much thought was given to who was there. As for this list, it was the biggest group that was killed in one place in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look at the second page of annex 10.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: It's one and the same group, except that the last names and the first names are different, and they suffered the same fate like the persons that I spoke of a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If I may for a moment return to your written statements. With the corrections that we have discussed, do these statements accurately reflect what you would say if you were asked questions today about the events in the statements?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I mean, what I said in my statement is something that I stand by. Some kind of an error or omission can always slip in, because wherever one works, one may make a mistake as well. However, I made an effort to have this statement be as balanced as possible. However, what I wish to say before this Court is -- well, if you allow me to do so, Your Honours. Things started happening in Mostar a lot earlier before the war and while things were being prepared, as it were. In 1989, the first rally was held in Nevesinje. In 1990, Jovic from Novo Pazova, I don't know his first name, he had a rally against the government that was in power, and nobody was really opposed --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me make sure I get an answer to my technical question so that before we run out of time I've given the Chamber all the information they need whether to decide to admit your statements into evidence. To the best of your knowledge, with the corrections we've made, are these statements accurate, and if I asked you the same questions again, would you give the information contained in the statements?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I said, when taking the oath, that I would say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and that is what I wrote as well, so I don't think that there is much to discuss about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, may I move these statements into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you may. Before the Trial Chamber settles this, I have a few follow-up questions to put to you. I'd like to go to the point and discuss your statement with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two parts to your statement; first of all, the arrival of the people in Nevesinje, and after that the events which are directly tied to what happened on the 21st of June. What I'm interested in is this: When you saw the various forces arriving in Nevesinje or its surroundings, or in the surrounding areas, what entitles you to say that, according to you, there were Chetniks, and who were the people who made up these Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: I grew up and to this day I live in a place where the phenomenon of Chetniks is not an unknown thing. As for the intentions and programmes of Chetnik programmes, we Bosniaks understand them to quite an extent. It wasn't only in this war. There were wars before this one, too. The Chetniks in Nevesinje, as a special formation with special objectives, that is something that did not exist. What existed was a programme of a Greater Serbia, and all the formations fought under a single banner. However, different tasks -- well, my objective over here is to clear the name of honest Serbs who did not sully their hands. However, I think that on the orders of military security, there were individuals who did a great deal of evil in Nevesinje. These were former communists and former JNA officers. I mentioned one of them, Parezanin. I did not mention others, but Blagoje Adzic was certainly involved in the area of Nevesinje. He's a general of the former JNA. He lives in Belgrade. I don't know whether he's retired or not, but he is related to some people in Nevesinje. The president of the Municipality of Nevesinje, Vukan Bratic was his name, he came after Bratic [as interpreted], he is probably related to this general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you say that the forces that attack were the following: The local police, the members of Karadjordje units, Karadjordje unit. I don't know who these people are. You say there was Arkan's unit and Seselj's unit. What I'm interested in is this: Seselj's unit. How do you know that these were Seselj's men or Seselj's units? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: When speaking of Seselj's unit, I know very little, but people could still move about. And these people who call themselves that, Seselj's men, or as they were designated Seselj's men, they instilled fear in the Serbs who did not want to respond to mobilisation or who cooperated in any other way with other ethnic groups. For me to have seen any one of them having killed someone or for me to know their names, I mean, they didn't really have names. They were called the Yellow One, the White One, the Man of Vukovar, the Man of Pozarevac. They had all sorts of nicknames like that. I'm not going into all their nicknames now. So, in this way, that was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you talk to these people? Did you speak to these people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: No, I did not talk to them at all. I didn't find them interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you say, the head of these men was someone going by the name of Parezanin? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Parezanin was the chief of military security who was in charge of all units. It wasn't only Karadjordje or whatever, Seselj's men. He was a JNA officer, of the former JNA, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you say he was a colonel in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, very well known to us in the talks, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you seem to be an educated man and you are now an elected official, I'm sure you are going to answer my question. In your view, this JNA colonel was the person who had authority over all the units present on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Let me make a correction. I am not a local counselman. I spent three terms as a local counselman, but my title is different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: He covered all units. As for commands and orders, there is no doubt about that. Tasks were issued as to who should do what. When there would be a snag, when people did not obey, well, one knew who would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get to the second part. You state that on the 21st of June, the villages of Postoljani, Donja Bijenja, and Gornja Bijenja were attacked, and you say that you saw this attack, since you had a pair of binoculars, and there were tanks and artillery fire, and you saw troops, groups of Chetniks, around the village. This large-scale attack, since there are attacks -- this is a large-scale attack, according to you, was this attack conducted under the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, Judge, on the 16th of June, below Mount Velez, on this plateau by Mostar, the Serbs suffered a terrible defeat, where the commander got killed, Pusara, commander of that sector, and in fact there was no line between Mostar and Nevesinje. On the 14th of June, before that, the village of Zulja was torched, then it was the municipality of Nevesinje, and now the area belongs to Mostar, and masses of people were taken out of that village. On the 16th of June, was attacked was the village of Odzak, and whoever happened to be there is not alive anymore. On the 21st of June, in the evening, Gornja and Donja Bijenja and Postoljani were attacked, and there was some artillery preparation before that. I was in the woods then. I was an armed man. I am a hunter. And at that time, I could not recognise who was a policeman, who was a man of Seselj's, who was this and who was that, but I'm convinced that they all took part because they had these big boom boxes and they were playing music. And you could also hear that they spoke the Ekavian dialect. Yet again on the same day, there was an ultimatum to us that we would return, that an attack would begin in an hour, and that we should hand over our weapons, the weapons we had, and that we should go back to continue normal life. Normal life in that kind of a situation, I mean, that is mindless, because there has been no normal life in Nevesinje since 1991, when the Uzice and Titograd Corps arrived. We had over 350 civilians who were fleeing at the time, and also from some other villages where the local Serbs helped us, Pluzine, Bratac, and in part of Odzak people were wandering about, and then they joined us, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are saying is already in your statement, sir. You're not answering my question. What I wanted to know was whether this attack had been conducted under the command of the JNA. It's either "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you lived through this attack, since you saw it, and then you say in your statement that you joined the Territorial Defence in Konjic and, in fact, you did not witness what happened after that, i.e., the crimes that were committed against the inhabitants that were taken captive. That, you don't know. You heard about this afterwards. Do we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: We fully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question now. And then I will ask my colleagues on the bench whether they have any questions to put to you. My last question has to do with Grahovac, Arsen Grahovac. Who is this person?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM KUJAN
utterances.text: This is the way it was: I knew Arsen Grahovac personally, he did not seem to be a bad person to me. However, in 1991, Radovan Sprema, who was an MP in the then Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or was it the Chamber of Citizens or was it the Chamber of Municipalities, as these things were called then, I don't know. But, anyway, with Arsen, he established this detachment that was named "Karadjordje," and also there was this coffee bar called "Ravna Gora." And then this detachment took up all the roads and all the exists from Nevesinje. People were mistreated practically, some of them were even beaten, some were searched. If a person would go there ten times a day, they'd be searched ten times a day. And there were cases when people were made to graze grass, and I don't want to go into all the things that happened. Arsen's defence, I know that. There are very few survivors, very few of his soldiers survived, and this detachment stopped functioning. It was established -- or, rather, what was established in Nevesinje was the Nevesinje Brigade. Novica Gusic was the commander, and he hails from Bratac. He's also a former JNA officer and lives somewhere in Belgrade nowadays. There was this man called Bratace. I don't know him at all. I didn't mention him in my statement. He was also the commander of this Nevesinje Brigade. As for Arsen, I really have nothing additional to say. In fact, this detachment was established by Sprema, and who issued tasks to Arsen Grahovac and the detachment, I assume -- I am I assume it was the Military and State Security, the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You anticipated my next question. I was going to ask you who Arsen Grahovac reported to. You said you didn't know, but you assumed that he reported to the military security bodies. Thank you for having answered the question I was about to put to you. I shall turn to my colleagues on the Bench and see if they have any questions. They don't. Since Mr. Seselj is not going to cross-examine you, I shall thank you, on behalf of my colleagues, for having come to testify in The Hague on those facts which you may have witnessed. Your statement will be admitted into evidence, and I shall ask the Registrar to give us an exhibit number, please. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I'm going to have a procedural matter to deal with before you assign a number to this statement, of course once the witness leaves. I don't think it is necessary for you to admit into evidence the statement in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness -- all this can be done in the absence of the witness, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If Mr. Seselj has an objection that can be cured by putting a particular question to the witness then we should take care of that now. I also wanted to raise the question if the Chamber wants the handwritten corrections to be made part of the record or if the verbal testimony is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please make your objection. If this needs to be checked in the presence of the witness, please go ahead. What is your objection, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with the witness. It is of a purely procedural nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has nothing to do with the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with the witness. It has something to do with the conduct of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with the witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are two statements involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have two, 2004 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are forcing me to present the essence of my objection before the witness, and I don't want that. I am not -- I don't want the witness to say what he has to say in view of my objections if I'm not examining him anyway. So it doesn't have to do with me; it has to do with formal objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you may now leave the courtroom, since this objection has nothing to do with the content of your statement. I shall ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been decided, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May we ask that the witness wait, in case there is information that Mr. Seselj is providing that is germane to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can deal with that afterwards, if need be. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor to address this procedural matter. Prior to that, nonetheless, we shall give an exhibit number to the 1998 statement. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P524.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not going to repeat my principled opposition to the application of Rule 92 ter. You all know my objections in regard to that. I am only going to point out here what you stated at one point, Mr. President. Your decision had to do with admitting this witness's statement from 1998 according to Rule 92 ter. In that statement, there is a single reference to Seselj's men. That is what you quoted, where he says the forces that were carrying out these attacks were the local police, members of the Karadjordje unit, Chetniks from Serbia and Montenegro, and Arkan's and Seselj's units that arrived in Nevesinje towards the end of 1991. I saw them personally. They socialized with Savic, the chief of police. They had special insignia. They wore red berets and they had insignia with white eagles. You accept that this goes into evidence. I mean, I'm not going to oppose that at all. However, that is the only reference to Seselj's men. Let us leave aside the fact that Arkan's men were never there, nor were there any of Seselj's men there, but let's leave that aside. In that area, there were never, ever any of Arkan's men. However, I'd like to draw your attention to the following, that what is stated here is that both Seselj's men and Arkan's men wore red berets, which is absolutely incredible. And then it says that Arkan's men had white eagles, which is not true, because Arkan had his own insignia. However, you admitted this statement from 1998. You admitted it into evidence, and you are going to assess its probative value. Now it is your own affair. You are in charge of assessing probative value of statements that are admitted into evidence. Now, on the basis of what do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why didn't you raise these issues in the presence of the witness? That would have enabled us to explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in that way it would look like cross-examination, and I do not wish in any way to legalize your decision that any statement be admitted according to Rule 92 ter. If I were to be involved in cross-examination, then I would be saying that you're right for admitting that into evidence, and I do not dare do that because that is the strategy of my defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have, I'm sure, clearly noted that I addressed this paragraph which mentions Seselj's men when I put my question to the witness, and I asked him what entitled him to say that these were Seselj's men, and you heard his answer. He said that people were saying that these were Seselj's men, or some people were saying it. That's all he said by way of an answer to my question. As far as the assessment is concerned, well, this will be weighed globally. We will not be satisfied with this statement only to assess what actually happened, who is responsible for what, which units were present, and so on and so forth. Of course, it didn't escape me that they had red berets. It didn't escape me that they wore white eagles, either. Of course, it goes without saying, so this will be weighed by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, hold on a second, because I wish to add, in continuation of what the Presiding Judge has just told you, that you can't, for your own strategic reasons, circumvent the procedural rules of this Court. You should have raised this issue while the witness was there, which would have enabled the Judges to explore the matter further. We asked you specifically whether your intervention had anything to do with the witness's statement, and you said, "No." And then when the witness had left, it turned out that it had everything to do with the statement. That is not a proper way of conducting your defence. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I believe that the Presiding Judge questioned the witness correctly with regard to this matter. I have no objections to raise in that context. Secondly, I believe that your decision is unlawful, in terms of applying 92 ter, because there is a provision in the Rules that says that newly-created amendments to the indictment cannot pertain to my case, and if -- and that prejudices me. And I certainly proved that that does prejudice me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are very well versed in procedural matters. The Trial Chamber has already settled the issue, the retractive application of 92 ter. This has already been settled. Fortunately, I know my case back to front, which means that I can answer your question. If I were an incapable judge, I would just let you speak, and everybody would be under the impression that your rights have been infringed, but the point you have just mentioned is a point which has been addressed many times by the Trial Chamber. I believe Mrs. Dahl had even responded. And despite that, despite the fact that Mrs. Dahl provided an answer, despite that the Trial Chamber has ruled on this, you are putting this on the agenda once again. We understand this full well, you feel this may prejudice you. We have clearly stipulated that there is no prejudice because you have the possibility to cross-examine. Since you do not wish to cross-examine, you have realised that the Bench, the Judges and I, go to the point. We put questions to the witness in this way, and this is what I did in this case also.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, you forced me to now repeat my earlier objections, but I haven't presented the gist of my current objection. The first one was the illustration -- will you please warn Mrs. Dahl not to interrupt me? That's an illustration. However, Mrs. Dahl is now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mr. Seselj, Mrs. Dahl is on her feet. Mrs. Dahl, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Seselj has not finished, so he still wants to add something. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm made to understand that we have a second witness remaining. There is a short amount of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the recess, we have to take a break. If there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj can file a written submission and explicate completely and clearly any new fact or new argument that he has yet to present to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Seselj, we have the second witness for today. He's waiting. And we will also have to take a break. If the latter part of your objection can be made very briefly, I will hand you the floor, but try to be brief, please. And after that, we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you decided to accept the 1998 statement under 92 ter, the Prosecution is now sneaking in another statement, saying it's just an amendment and a correction of the previous one, whereas I'm convinced that if you had had insight into this statement of 2004, you would have never decided that this witness testify under 92 ter. You would have brought him viva voce. That is the gist of my objection, because in this 2004 statement he's presenting new assertions that he'd never featured before. And here in paragraph 4 -- sorry, 7, he said I was in Nevesinje in summer 1991, and now he's correcting himself, saying it was the beginning of 1992. It's a huge lapse of time. It can't be a simple, genuine mistake. And then he says for a fact Seselj appointed and authorised Arsen Grahovac as the leader of the unit that was always in combat readiness, whereas I showed you that he was a deputy of the Serbian Renewal Movement. If you think it's not in the interests of justice to allow me to present this, you will drop me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I did not understand. You also wanted the other statement to be put in record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. The 2004 statement is actually not going to be admitted. In fact, it's the 1998, not the other one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is really so, then my objection is pointless. I had understood that you were admitting both statements, because the second one was presented by Ms. Dahl as an amendment and a corrective of the previous one. If only the first statement is going in, not the one from 2004, then my objection doesn't stand, but I would like to hear from Ms. Dahl. Does she want both statements admitted or just the one from 1998? If she confirms that she tendered only the 1998 statement, then it's all right, but I'm certain that she tendered both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did tender both, because there are corrections in the 2004 statement that go to the 1998 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. The Trial Chamber decides to admit the 1998 statement. And with regard to some details and some points of the 1998 statements, that's in the transcript. So we have the 1998 statement, plus the transcript which deal with some corrections; the fact that it was not in the summer of 1991, but that it was in 1992. The changes are on the transcript. So we are going to take a 20-minute break, and we will reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I need the portion of the second statement that includes the list of victims, or we can simply admit annex 10 as identified by the witness, because the 2004 statement lists out the people who were killed from the various villages. And if I had appreciated the Chamber was going to reject the 2004 statement, I would have led that orally so that we could get that into the record. If I may just -- I can write a very brief written submission about the key pieces for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what is your concern is basically the list of victims, the annex 10, if I'm not mistaken, but that is already in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, I have to prove the indictment. I can't simply rest on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, but it's in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: But if I may, I want to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, but -- one moment, please. But in the transcript, the person did confirm the list. He did confirm the list, so there is no problem, is there? So you are seeking the admission of the list, such as recognised by the witness from his statement. But I will confer with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, Judges, I can assist you. I am not contesting the existence of these victims and the list of victims, because I don't believe anyone would make up a list of people who were killed. So I'm not challenging that. What matters to me is that you confirm to me that the statement from 2004 was not admitted into evidence, because if it had been admitted, that would have been unlawful, in my opinion. That was the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's give an exhibit number to the list. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the list, which is annex 10 to the indictment, will be Exhibit number P525.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With regard, Your Honour, to the 2004 statement, there are a number of paragraphs that go directly to the prior statement to correct or augment information, in particular the lists of people who were killed, and I believe that Your Honour covered the information about Arsen Grahovac. But I think in the interests of having complete information before the Chamber, I would prefer that you admit it and then determine what weight to give it. I think his testimony did cover the mosques and the church destructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We have already decided. First of all, we are admitting the 1998 statement, then the list of annex 10 recognised by the witness is also admitted. Thirdly, the corrections that were made regarding the 1998 statement are in the transcript, and that's all. We will reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me in a language that you understand? Very well. We will ask you to read the solemn declaration. But before that, please give us your name, your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nebojsa Stojanovic, born on the 28th of July, 1966, in Vranje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed, sir, and if so, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I work in the finance section of a private business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you an accountant? What do you do, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Financial manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you ever testified before a tribunal regarding the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or are you testifying for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated. Witness, before I hand the floor to the Prosecutor, I would like to inform you on the way the hearing will take place. This is a -- these proceedings may different than the ones you're accustomed to in your own country. First, what will happen is you will first have to answer to questions that will be put to you by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor may also show you some documents. We have two hours for this portion. Then Mr. Seselj, the accused, sitting to your left, will also put questions to you in cross-examination, and Mr. Seselj will also dispose of the same amount of time as the Prosecutor. The three Judges sitting before you will also be able to intervene at any point in time, and we may also put questions to you. Please try to be concise in answering questions put to you, and if you do not understand a question, please ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it or to put the question again. Every 90 minutes, we take a 15- or 20-minute break. This allows the witness to rest, because you will see that it can be tiresome to answer questions, and also we may change -- or we have to change the tapes, actually. And if you are tired at any point in time, please tell us and we will give you a break. And we are also here to answer any question or concern that you may have. You are now sworn in and you are a Court witness, which means that up until tomorrow, the end of your testimony, you're not to have any contacts with anybody except, of course, with members of your family to tell them that you're all right and that everything is going well. Other than that, you may not discuss this case with anybody. I also notice that you took out some documents from your purse or case. What are those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say that I have certain problems that started back in Serbia, and I've been here for a couple of days. Second, I officially stated before this International Tribunal that I want to be a Defence witness, and I documented this. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber received this documentation, authorised and verified officially in court, because there is a little difference between the judicial procedure, so I verified this statement in court. After hearing from you, I am in two minds now. I don't want to violate any of your rules or be accused of contempt by failing to appear. On the other hand, I have medical certificates that I have great health problems, because the gentlemen from the Prosecution are exerting great pressure on me and my family. We have tried to do something about it through my lawyers, but I received no answer from the president. Instead, I got a new summons, so it is new pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'm glad you came, because if you hadn't come, we would have had to make an indictment against you, and you would have ended up in jail. So I am very glad you answered the injunction to appear. Now, we knew that you wanted to be a Defence witness, except that the witnesses do not believe -- do not belong to the Defence or to the Prosecution. You are a witness of the justice, of the Court, and the Prosecutor deemed that you are to answer questions that he will put to you. But the procedure calls for the fact that if the Prosecutor sees that you are not answering his questions, then he will state that you are a hostile witness. And then he will have the right to put you leading -- to put leading questions to you, because this procedure is the common law procedure and witnesses of the Prosecutor have to answer in a neutral way -- rather, the Prosecutor will put neutral questions. He cannot lead an answer or get an answer from you or from any witness. Now, if you are a hostile witness or if he deems that you are a hostile witness, the Prosecutor may inform the Chamber of the fact that he believes that you are a hostile witness, and then he is allowed to put other questions -- other types of questions to you, leading questions. For the time being, you are here to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution, by Mr. Seselj, and by the Judges of this Trial Chamber. You will answer on facts that you have witnessed. Maybe what you say will go in favour of Mr. Seselj. Good for him. But it can also be in favour of the Prosecution. Good for them. But what the Judges of this Trial Chamber wish is that you answer so that we can get closer to truth. Now you're under oath. You've stated that you will tell the truth, and nothing else but the truth. This is what counts. Whether your testimony goes in favour of one party or another, that is not our problem. That is somebody else's problem, if you will. However, you told me that you do not feel well, that you have health problems. If at any point in time you are not feeling well, you have to let me know, and then we will call a doctor to examine you. But since you are taken care of by the Witness and Victims Section, I'm sure that you must have told them that you are suffering, that you're not well, and I'm sure that they must have brought this to the attention of the doctor. You seem well to me. Maybe in the following seconds you will get a heart attack, but I can also die of a heart attack in a few seconds. I cannot foresee this. But for the time being, you seem quite capable to answer questions that will be put to you. But if you are not feeling well, please let me know and we will stop. Now, your medical chart you may keep for you, because it is covered by medical secrecy. If you wish, you can tell us what medical problems you have - that's up to you - but I am not authorised to ask you what your health problems are, precisely, what you are suffering from. Now, you've talked about pressure. Now, I imagine that the Prosecutor may have called you on a couple of occasions to ask you to come, and I'm sure that he may have -- he must have told you that if you don't appear before this Court, you will suffer the consequences. I was not there, I did not witness the conversation, I don't know what the Prosecutor may have told you, but maybe it's just a friendly pressure. What really is important, actually, is that you are here. And also what's important, it is important for Mr. Seselj, because he will be putting questions to you, and this is for his defence, and this is why it is important that you also answer his questions. Since you are under oath, you are now a witness of the Court. This is what I wanted to tell you. Maybe I've reassured you. I hope I did. Do you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to fear, because I trust the Court and I trust you, the Judges. However, I suffer from angina pectoris. I have brought all the documentation on that, testifying to how poorly I'm feeling. But as you've said, I did give the solemn declaration, and I'm willing to testify. But I would like to testify once that contact is made with the Defence of Mr. Vojislav Seselj. The first statement that I gave to the Prosecution and which I signed, it's true that I signed it without looking, because I was verbally informed of the contents; but it's actually very different from what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, but that's not really a problem, because you came to answer questions. So your statement is not going to be taken into account. This is not a type of trial where your statement will be admitted. When the Prosecutor puts questions to you, you will tell him exactly what happened, according to you. So maybe you will contradict your own statement. That doesn't matter. What really matters is that you will have to answer the questions that are put to you. You received your statement because I suppose that Mr. Seselj's Defence must have sent it to you. You reread it and then you realised that what it contains does not correspond either to what you said or to reality, so you are here to explain it, in fact. And you will explain this for justice. Maybe it's going to be in the interests of Mr. Seselj, maybe it's in the interests of the Prosecutor, I don't know, but we will see. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojanovic. My name is Mathias Marcussen. I'm a trial attorney for the Prosecution. As you did not wish to meet any of the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor after you arrived in The Hague, we have not had a chance to meet. As the President pointed out, I'm going to ask some questions about events in 1991. The Presiding Judge noted that you have some documents, and I can see you still have them in front of you. For the purpose of the testimony, I think the best would be if you would be kind enough to put your documents aside and just answer my questions, and I might show you some documents along the way. But it would be better if you wouldn't mind putting your notes away, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question, actually, for the witness. I wasn't seeing you very well, because in fact I have two screens. I see you have an emblem on your pullover or on your T-shirt. What is it? Is that a football club, or what is it, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Serbian coat of arms of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you please put all your documents away. But it's fine that you lie them down next to you. I'm not asking for them to be taken from you, but it would be better if you would be kind enough to place them next to you, please.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know, what's the problem with the judiciary of Serbia? There is documentation, and I'm keeping all this. It was all a long time ago, and I'm keeping this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, but in our judicial system - this is an international criminal tribunal - this is an oral procedure, so the witness has to answer orally. Very well. So please set aside the documents that you have before you. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to start asking you whether you have done your military service.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in what unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Armoured Mechanised Unit in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 1985/1986, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after your military service, did you pursue any studies?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What did you study?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from a higher school in Vranje. Later in Pristina, I graduated from the School of Science and Mathematics from the University of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I should tell you, sir, as we haven't talked about how our evidence should go, that I'm pausing a little bit. That's because we have translations, so it's not that I'm doubting your answers. I'm just allowing the translators to translate. After your military service, did you have a job somewhere? And if so, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did this higher school in Serbia, the evening course, and that's the same I did with the university. It was like on-the-job training or parallel -- studies parallel with work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the studies you did in Pristina, did you obtain a university degree? And if so, at what level?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I received a diploma of Bachelor of Chemistry and Mathematics in 1999, so I have a university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It was -- maybe I misunderstood, but after your military service, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before my military service, I had already started working. That was in 1995 [as interpreted]. I started working in the shoe factory, Kostana. And in Serbia, when you are 18 or 19, you apply to do your military service, which lasts for a year, and during that time your job is on hold, waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you came back from your military service, in what function did you work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after that, when I completed that school, I was an ordinary blue-collar worker, but I got promoted gradually; first, manager, and then to the chief of the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How long were you the chief of the laboratory?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A year, perhaps. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after that, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, the business was not doing well, and after 1990, it went bankrupt. I became later the general manager of a company in Bujanovac, a factory producing batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how long did you serve as the general manager?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until 2004. The 21st of January, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after 2004, what have you been done since then?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Belgrade to live there. I got married. I worked in Galenika, a pharmaceutical factory, for two years, and then I moved to another company, INVE, in Zemun, near Belgrade. And now I'm working in the business I've already mentioned in answering the Judge's question in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just have to clarify a question -- or an answer that you gave. It says on the transcript that you started to work already in 1995. Would I be correct that it's actually in 1985?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So that will be a correction to line 25 on page 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I completed the high school at 18, and I immediately got that job. There was some different sections, different vocational orientations, and every graduate immediately got a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And we understand that you have made quite a good career for yourself since then. I just wondered, what languages do you speak? Do you speak any other languages than Serbian?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I speak French, and since 1999, after the NATO aggression in Serbia, I stopped using French completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we will maybe get back to this later, but I just wanted to clarify something before we go into your evidence. Am I correct that you have given a number of statements to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you gave two statements in 2004 and one statement in 2006; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, as we didn't get a chance to meet, I wondered, have you had a chance to review those statements before you came here today?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed them. I reviewed them, but I told even the Presiding Judge that there are certain things that I have not said and that are contained in the statement. So the statement is different from what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I see. Maybe we'll get back to some of those issues, and maybe not. I will ask you some questions -- I'm basing my questions on what I know of your evidence from these statements, so that's the basis for the questions. But we will see whether I have understood things correctly or not. Did you receive call-up papers from the army in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you receive any call-up papers at any point in time from the army?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you served in the army since you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1999, at the time of the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you -- do you know of a training camp in a location called Erdut?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you ever been there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When were you there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was October. I gave a letter to the investigators, officially. It's a military certificate. October 1991, but I was there briefly, perhaps a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: October of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did you go after you had been in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They turned us back, "us," meaning the group of people who were with me. Maybe later you'll want me to explain which group of people it was. They turned us back to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, yes, what was that group of people?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a group of people from Vranje where, in 1990, 1991, after the multiparty elections and the establishment of new parties, we had formed the Serbian National Renewal, and the objective was to form the Serbian Chetnik Movement. We had a great number of followers who wanted to take part on the frontline to defend Serbian lands as part of the army and units of the Territorial Defence in the region where we were sent under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So how many -- how big was this group you were with?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so you went to Sid, and where did you go after Sid?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
