utterances.text: From Sid, first we had to go to Lipovaca woods, where the Territorial Defence of Slovenia, Western Slovenia and Baranja, and Western Srem sent us. First we had to go to a battery of exams to see if people were in good health, whether they had any army training, whether they knew how to handle weapons, whether they had training, because it was a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At some point did you come to -- did you come to the area of Vukovar with this group of people?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A few days, we were in the Lipovaca forest, where we received certain weapons and some training was conducted, and a number of people had to go back primarily due to fear. People did not know whether this was a war zone. Some people came there for other reasons; to loot, to steal. So they understood how serious this was. A few days after the training, we went to Vukovar. Buses were organised for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you came to Vukovar, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not report to anyone. We were a group that had reported to the responsible person at Petrova Gora. In our group in Lipovaca forest, there were other volunteers from other towns in Serbia, so we met most of these people the first time then. And we had a leader who then reported us to their Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question. I followed what you were saying very carefully. You said that together with other volunteers, you were sent to Vukovar, but from what I understand, this was something personal which you did on your own behalf. At the time, did you have a membership card indicating that you belonged to a political party or were you just fighting for your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already mentioned that in Vranje, we had established the Serb National Revival Movement. Mr. Mirko Jovic was president, and we were pretty extremist in terms of the Chetnik movement. You know what the Chetnik movement is. These are people who continue the tradition of the Chetniks from the Second World War who defended the country. And within our organisation, there was an internal organisation; namely, that people were sent to territories where the country would be defended or, rather, where the unprotected Serb people would be defended. That is how we set out. Our headquarters were in Belgrade. The commander was Zoraja, and that was somewhere in the street of Kneza Milosa, near Jugobanka. Some offices that were there was rather disorganized. They gave us papers to go to Erdut. I mentioned already that the gentleman from the Territorial Defence returned us to Sid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having clarified this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, under -- once you had come to the area of Vukovar, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned in my previous remarks that we became organised at Petrova Gora, and then we were organised so as to be in the first line, in terms of guarding certain streets and houses, because there was a war conflict going on there and the army -- or, rather, appropriate formations that were freeing one street after another, I mean, we would take up their positions because they would be withdrawing. So we were guarding their houses -- or, rather, the houses that they had liberated so that armed Croats would not return there from the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, and all of those who carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you serving under -- were you volunteers, were you part of the Territorial Defence, or where did you belong in the armed forces that were in the area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the complete list of these persons who came as volunteers joined the Yugoslav People's Army that was there was. There was full control of these units of volunteers, if I can call them that, and they were fully organised, but independently from the army; that is to say that they had their appropriate zone and their appropriate commander who commanded them, that is to say, those volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean Kameni and Kinez, but I don't really know them. I never even saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the SRS there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, we were all in that unit, and quite simply no one could say that he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party, or of the SPO, or of whatever other party. I just know that most people that were there were Serbs and from the area, that is to say, Vukovar, Borovo Selo, Bobota and the surrounding area, because they were familiar with the area. And that is how we were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you were in the area, did you witness the capture of any Croatians, people from the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Never. Perhaps later in Velepromet, if that means anything to you, if you want me to tell you about that now. But as for these activities, the war conflict during that month before the liberation of Vukovar, I did not see any such thing, because we took up these buildings and we could not follow the units that were liberating Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did Kameni give any orders regarding where any prisoners that might have been taken -- where those prisoners should be taken to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of anything like that. I repeat once again, we were never in contact. We had some kind of a leader of our own, who told us where we would be staying, in which houses, because there were five or six of us per house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you ever witness the killing of any people who had been captured in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While you were in Vukovar, did you ever witness the killing of any people who had been captured?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I witnessed something like that once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you describe that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to explain it to you now. I mentioned a few moments ago, after the fall of Vukovar -- can I talk about that now? Most of the forces were withdrawn from Vukovar, whereas most of the people -- how should I put this? The people who were locals, from Vukovar, I mean, they stayed on at Velepromet. Due to the condition of my health, I was also transferred to Velepromet because the conditions were somewhat better there, the living conditions. So I could follow most of the people who were brought in after the fall of Vukovar to Velepromet for some kind of a check. I mean, they looked at their IDs. They released some people and detained others, probably in order to receive some intelligence as to what was going on and whether any of these Croats had committed some misdeeds or crimes within Vukovar during the siege of Vukovar by the Serbs or, rather, before this conflict started between the Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did any of -- my question was whether you had seen anyone get killed. Are you saying that in this context, somebody got killed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. 90 per cent of these people I already mentioned from Vukovar, they held Velepromet. I mean, they questioned these Croats, interrogated them; women, children. They knew each other before the war, before the conflict that broke out in Vukovar. I remember one night it so happened right before my very own eyes, these people from Vukovar whom I did not know, they got this man out and they killed him in Velepromet; that is to say, outside, there was screaming, things like that. No one could have helped this person. I couldn't have helped him, either, because I don't know these people and I don't know what would have happened to me. However, when the army found out, on the very next day automatically they placed their own security there, and no one was allowed to enter Velepromet after that, none of these -- what do I call these people? These people from Vukovar, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was after the fall of Vukovar, in the month of November. Perhaps November, December, something like that. I can't remember. It's been a long time now. I'm a bit of an emotional person. Perhaps I was not really cut out for the front. What can I say to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did Kameni ever issue any orders to kill Croat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already mentioned, in the context of the previous question, that I did not even know who Kameni was. I saw him on television perhaps a year or two ago in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you ever witness SRS volunteers kill Croats that had been captured?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying once again that I didn't see or know any SRS volunteers there, and I did not see them killing, because I did not have any possibility of seeing that. I wasn't at the frontline, I was guarding these houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor is going fast. It is important to put this in the right context. If I understand correctly, you were part of a group of people, of four to five people, and you had a leader. What was the name of the leader of this small group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall. A man from Borovo Selo. I can't remember. Mirko or something like that. I mean, he gave us instructions as to which house we would stay at, what we would do, how we would stand guard duty, how we would guard these positions, because we changed every two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you were standing guard at night or during the day, did you ever fight, did you ever fire shots at the enemy, or were you patrolling and standing guard and you never fired a single shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never fired. We never had occasion to do so, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you take anyone prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't have, because we didn't take part in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you patrol around Vukovar? Did you patrol through the streets? Did you go to check-points, and did you meet other fighters, other Serb fighters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the way it was: We could not patrol because we were at Leva Supoderica. It was Milovo Brdo, that's what it was called. We were guarding houses, and every two or three days, we would see army troops passing by, continuing to advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the exception of the small group of people headed by Mirko, did you ever discuss or talk to these people from Leva Supoderica to discuss the war with them, to talk about the weather? Did you ever talk to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you met other fighters, did some believe they were volunteers of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have occasion to do so. Most of these people were illiterate, and as time went by, I mean, we lived there together with these people every day and then I realised why it was they had come there in the first place, but they'd never said so. They were interested in stealing, searching, because the army, as they were liberating one house after the other, then we would -- they would withdraw and we would take those houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, these volunteers that were standing guard, they were patrolling around and occupying the houses, you are saying that when the army left, you played your part, and it is then, seemingly, that some people started looting, pilfering, or doing I don't know what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among those people doing this, did people say that some of these people were volunteers of the SRS or was this something you heard about afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I never heard that. Most of these -- let me call them that, "volunteers," they were locals, and it suited them because they knew which house was a Croatian house and which house was a house of wealthy people. Then we would even put away some valuables so that they wouldn't be stolen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, concerning the volunteers in the broader sense of the meaning, I'm talking now in percentage terms: How many of them were locals and how many people came from elsewhere? Could you give me a figure, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. From day to day, as the fall of Vukovar was becoming imminent, more and more locals were coming back to Vukovar, people who left their families in Serbia, and they asked to be at the frontline, either out of revenge or for some other reason. I don't know about that. I just know that my team, consisting of five or six men, we were there up until the very end, and that is when we went our separate ways, when we parted from this man from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At some point, out of the hundred people on the ground, how many came from Vukovar and the surrounding area, compared with people who came from Belgrade or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sixty to forty, let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying 60 to 40 per cent were locals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am saying 60 per cent were from Vukovar and 40 per cent were the people who came from elsewhere. So the number was going down. Part of the volunteers returned to Serbia, trying to find different ways and means, seeing that things were so difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While you were in Vukovar, did you see Mr. Seselj at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You never saw Seselj in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Never, because, I mean, I did not have a situation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short question, Witness. You are an educated man. You studied mathematics. When you arrived in Vukovar, had you heard Mr. Seselj's name before? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I mean -- I mean, that wasn't the question. I mean, I heard Seselj earlier on, on the political scene, and then there was this rally in Vranje. And I knew he was president of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was a well-known figure, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not personally, not that way, because we are a party that did not recognise the Serbian Radical Party. Our volunteers were volunteers of the Chetnik movement. We did not recognise those volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, as a matter of fact. At that time, we even imposed a name on Mr. Vojislav Seselj, saying that he was the red vojvoda. So there was no close relationship between the SRS and our Chetnik movement, the SNS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why was he a red vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we believed that at the time of the regime of Slobodan Milosevic, Mr. Seselj was on good terms with Mr. Milosevic, and we were fighting for the old Serbia, the return to old borders. Let me say that we advocated -- our party advocated that old Serbia from way back, from the times of the king, and we wanted the king to come back to Serbia. That is the kind of ideology that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you yourself, were you a royalist, a monarchist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For many years or did you turn royalist in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, a lot earlier. We still believe that a monarchy will come back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Seselj did not embody your royalist aspirations, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I understand you didn't see Mr. Seselj in Vukovar. Did you hear from anyone that he was present in Vukovar in -- while you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one moment, I heard that he had come to visit the frontline, because as I have already said, we were not exactly on the frontline and we heard information coming through the loudspeakers, and I recognised Mr. Vojislav Seselj's voice very well. He was asking the Croats, those who had taken up weapons, who had bloodied their hands and all others, that they surrender so as to avoid further bloodshed in Vukovar. Well, why would a city fall with thousands and thousands of people getting killed? That was my idea with regard to this. So he wanted to avoid a large number of casualties on the Croat side and on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are now discussing something which is important to us. You have just mentioned this, but I would like you to be very accurate. As far as you remember, well, of course, this happened 15 years ago, I'm the first person to admit this, but as far as you remember, what were the exact words uttered by Mr. Seselj? Either you can answer this question accurately or you can only answer it in vague terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember. I know that it was -- I mean over this loudspeaker that was on a combat vehicle of the army. This call was addressed to all Croats, all those who had weapons in their hands; that is to say, all of those who fought on the Croat side in defending the town, they were called upon to surrender, and they were to be treated in accordance with the International Conventions on Prisoners, and that they should surrender as soon as possible because every day is increasingly difficult for the Serbs and for all of those who are under siege. I mean, it's been a very long time. I mean, there were no signs of hatred that somebody should get killed or something like that. I didn't hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you quite sure that he said, "Surrender and you will be treated according to international treaties"? Are you quite sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure, because every day up until the fall of Vukovar, things were getting increasingly difficult on the Croat side and on our side, I think, because the Croats were defending the town desperately. I'm not saying Croat civilians, but people who had weapons in their hands. Later on I realised that Croats within Vukovar who held weapons, who carried weapons, I mean, even those Croats who wanted to leave Vukovar, I mean the Croats who carried weapons would shoot at their fellow countrymen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the command post a Nova Ulica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Seselj ever there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I suppose he was because the military command was there and anybody that was going to the territory and the town of Vukovar had to be identified and checked, who he was and what he was doing there, because the authorities of the JNA ruled there. They commanded -- they led the whole operation of the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You said you don't remember. Now, you gave a statement -- or you gave three statements to OTP, to the Office of the Prosecutor, as we discussed earlier. One of these statements from 2006 I'd like to read a passage from and ask you if that might refresh your recollection on this. In your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, according to your own practice, on which you insisted when we heard some other witnesses, this is an impermissible way of refreshing the witness's memory. You specified very exactly how a witness's memory may be jogged, but we have not even come to a point where the witness's memory has to be refreshed. This is an attempt to suggest to the witness something that the Prosecutor had written in the first place, as if the witness had written it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Marcussen, when we proceed to the refreshing of the memory, that's a common law procedure, so the Prosecutor should remind the witness that he stated something. You can only remind a witness of something that he doesn't remember anymore, so you first have to put to him a question on a topic, and if the witness already stated something very clearly on that topic and if he answers something else, and if there's a discrepancy between the two, then you can ask him, "Are you quite sure of what you are saying today?" And then, only then, you can show him a prior text, and then you can tell him, "This is what you said in such-and-such a year."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness says, as page 61, line 2: "I don't remember, but I suppose ..." And then he says what his supposition is. That is quite different from the earlier statement, as a number of other points have been here today. So I think we have established that the witness has said that he has an issue -- there's an issue of whether or not he might remember some facts. I'm happy to lay the foundation more specifically as to whether or not the statement was before him, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. So you can put to the witness that he answered something, and you can say, "You don't remember now, but in 2000-and-something you said this," so then you can say to him -- tell him what he said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I was just about to do when the accused made his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In 2006, you state at paragraph 43 of your statement, after speaking about the incident with a loudspeaker, you say: "Afterward, at the command of Nova Ulica, where the guards regiment was located, Vojislav Seselj had a meeting with the command officers allegedly to discuss joint actions of the JNA and the volunteers in the final operations of Vukovar. Vojislav Seselj stayed there half an hour/an hour. Vojislav Seselj left Vukovar the same day. "While we are on the subject, every day there were Chetnik music played over big speakers mounted on an armoured vehicle as well as recordings of Seselj's messages for Croats to surrender peacefully because of the JNA and the volunteers would sooner or later liberate Vukovar and their lives would be spared. "I did not see Vojislav Seselj commanding volunteers in Vukovar. His role was to organise them and boost their morale." And that's the end of that paragraph. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I emphasised to the Presiding Judge that I am astounded -- I was astounded to see my statement, because I hadn't received that statement from the Prosecution at the time when I gave it, because at that time that statement was not placed in the context of the Seselj trial. I emphasised that certain things in it were not correct, and that's why I came here in the first place, to tell the real thing to the Court. Even the statement that I read is in Croatian, it's not in my language, Serbian. I don't use the Croatian word for "train" or "vessel," and the whole thing made me sick because I know that's not the statement I gave. The thing that was read out to me was completely different, but trusting the investigators who read it out to me, I signed the statement, and that's one of the reasons why we are here today, to prove the truth and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to Erdut. Were you in Erdut in July or August 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While you were in Erdut, did you ever see Arkan there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of October, as I said, I gave the OTP an official certificate stating when I was sent to the frontline, for those two or three days, and that's when I saw him, because when we were there we had no access to that military installation. Ordinary soldiers and reservists were not allowed to go in there or walk about. We had a totally different base in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you -- did you see Mr. Seselj in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was there for only two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person called Radovan Stojisic, also known as Peca [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you ever deployed in Borovo Selo as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party -- you mean the Serbian Radical Party? 1994 or, rather, 1996, part of the Serbian National Revival collectively joined the Serbian Radical Party. I had left it for a couple of months because, as I said, my idea of Greater Serbia and the kingdom cannot fit with the idea of the Serbian Radical Party and the ideas of Mr. Seselj, who fought for a republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SRS in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I emphasised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier a rally that took place in Vranje. When was that rally?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1991. I don't remember whether it was in the month of May. My people and I from the Serbian National Revival stood there on the side, observing the rally, observing Mr. Seselj. There were followers of that Serbian Renewal Movement there as well, lots of people attending the rally, but I wasn't interested in that. I just came to see whether they had changed their policy towards the Serbian Chetnik Movement. That was the only thing that mattered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did Seselj give a speech at the rally?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the party leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember what he said on the speech?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the standard thing; you know, he was promoting the Serbian Radical Party because this municipal board was very young, it was in the process of being established, and he was doing the propaganda written into his programme and the plan of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember anything he said?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. It was quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a small point. I'm curious to know this. You said that you were a royalist, that you were a member of the Serb Renewal Movement. Why was there a meeting in 1991? Why did he hold a rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went just out of curiosity to see who was going to attend the meeting. Vranje is a small place, and this multiparty life -- how shall I put it? Everybody was curious to see and to take part. You know that at that time the ruling party was the party of Slobodan Milosevic, including in Vranje, and the reds held 90 per cent, as we put it; but even they came to hear Vojislav Seselj. My leader also came to Vranje to present our programme, the plan of our party to get into the Assembly and gain the maximum of seats. But I came really out of curiosity, because even the Serbian Renewal Movement representatives came to that rally and they caused an incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, at the rally when Mr. Seselj made a speech, did he refer to the concept of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The way I understand it, he was talking about Karlobag, Virovitica, Vrace borders, that region, because Serbian people lived in those lands and the Serbian Radical Party in Serbia itself should take care of those defenceless people. And I would, of course, accept it if my own party leader said the same thing; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj use the word "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did he -- did he refer to Thompsons or radical Thompsons; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, since you can't remember, I'd like to read out a part of the statement that we talked about before for you. It's from paragraph 7 of the statement, and a little down in the paragraph you say: "At the rally, Vojislav Seselj boosted from the rostrum that radical Thompsons were in action and that Ustasha at Borovo Selo were killed. The Thompsons was a World War II-era machine-gun. By "Ustasha," Seselj referred to all Croats." Now that I've read this to you, does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember, but it's a bit funny when you say that "Ustasha" was applied in reference to all Croats. Very often you hear the word "Chetnik" in this courtroom. It turns out that all of us Serbs are Chetniks. You can't hold up that argument, and similarly not all Croats can be Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Greater Serbia issue, I would just like to make sure what is it exactly you heard. Can you tell us if Mr. Seselj, in his speech, spoke of Greater Serbia as a goal to reach, that -- was he encouraging to take territories in order to create that famous line Karlobag-Virovitica, or was he on the other hand only referring to the Serbs who were living in that area in order to protect them, which is of course not the same thing? So as far as you remember, what was the speech exactly about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point of his discourse was to invoke, in fact, all the time the statute of his party, speaking about how the party is functioning, and that those Serbs needed to be protected over there because they are the majority population in Croatia. But there was no reference to volunteers in the battlefield, but I didn't hear that anybody was called upon to go there with rifles or Thompsons or anything else to defend anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that when he was speaking, he was applauded, or was he booed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me say that people were clapping, but, you know, at that time the television had such an influence on the people, on popular masses in the beginning of the conflict that was starting in the territory of the former SFRY, whereas we were not empowered to be able to create this media policy. People in Serbia are strange. There's always turmoil and dithering. If Mirko Jovic would have come to speak, people would have clapped equally, so people have their own opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as you remember, which impression did you get after hearing Mr. Seselj speak about the means that one should use to defend Serbs in that area? At what cost? How did he intend to do all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back again to that point. Our thinking, if you wish my thinking at that point, was not very serious concerning the Serbian Radical Party. I thought it was not serious to suggest that the Serbian Radical Party should go there and defend them. It's the official authorities who should take care of that. It was silly, in my opinion, to think that we volunteers could change anything. We were too small, in the perspective of all that was happening with these political stresses between Milosevic and Tudjman, and neither we nor the accused were in power. We had no influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But according to you, Mr. Seselj shared that opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a bit frivolous, in my opinion. It was just party propaganda, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question: You were present there in the month of May of 1991. So Mr. Seselj gave a speech. We know that also other people took the floor. And he was applauded. You say that he was applauded because he wanted to defend the Serb population. But from where you were standing, as a listener - you are a loyalist, monarchist, we know, you told us - did you get the feeling that Milosevic was an opponent to Mr. Seselj? Did you have that feeling? Did you have the feeling that Mr. Seselj was actually giving a speech against Milosevic or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I was a young politician at that time. I'm 43 now, and this was a long time ago. At that time, I was a student, and I wasn't able to understand anything. There were some opponents there, and that's why a scandal broke out at the rally. It's my opinion that it was more about party propaganda than about sending volunteers to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. You said that earlier. There was a scandal during that meeting. What happened exactly? You said it once already, but now you're repeating it. What was the problem exactly, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we are now going back. There was another group, another party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, led by Vuk Draskovic, and they were much more extreme in their approach to the Ustasha movement and the Croatian people, and they thought that this whole rally held by Mr. Vojislav Seselj is more political, it was more about promoting the Serbian Radical Party in Vranje, and they were shouting, "Duce, Duce," which was to mean that Vojislav Seselj was an autocrat within his party. And then a brawl started. They threw things towards the rostrum. This group I'm speaking of is another group that sent volunteers to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were saying "Duce, Duce," comparing him to Mussolini?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, they were shouting that to Mr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Marcussen, do you think we should take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now is fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to make some submission regarding the evidence of this witness, and I would ask -- I think it's best if the witness is not in the courtroom while we have those arguments. So maybe we can have him removed for a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, please stay behind the door with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has departed from his previous statements in aspects which are material to the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution believes that the witness is adverse now to telling what he has said was the truth before. The Prosecution, therefore, will seek leave to change the modalities of questioning of the witness and be allowed to cross-examine the witness. There is jurisprudence that supports this, that we can do this in the Popovic decision, which is a decision from the Appeals Chamber in the case of the Prosecutor versus Popovic and others in the case IT-05-88-AR-73.3. The title of the decision is "Decision on appeal against decision on impeachment of party's own witness" from the 1st of February this year. We would also at the end be seeking admission of the witness's prior statements into evidence. I say that the witness has departed from his previous statement on a number of material points, and I'd like to just go through some of the main points. But essentially the witness has departed from his -- the totality of the evidence he has in his earlier statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, just to shed some light on all of this, as far as I know it's not because a witness is a hostile witness that this necessarily means that his written statement should be admitted. What case law are you relying on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The point is that the -- well, it's not that the witness is adverse to the Prosecution in his demeanour or anything like that. The witness is, in our submission, departing from the truth in his testimony today. He is adverse to telling the truth. The truth is in his statements that he had earlier given to the Prosecution, and in my examination I will go through the statements and some issues to illustrate that to Your Honours. In the Popovic case, at paragraph -- in the decision of the Popovic case at paragraph 28 -- no, sorry, that's incorrect. At paragraph 31, the Appeals Chamber made clear that a Trial Chamber may admit a prior statement as substantive evidence also from a witness who had testified before a Trial Chamber. And the same is found in -- sorry, a decision from Trial Chamber II in the Limaj case, decision on the Prosecution's motion to admit statements as substantive evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall look into the matter later. Just, Mr. Seselj, two minutes you have now to raise your objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems to me that the Prosecutor took a bit longer. First of all, there is absolutely no grounds to declare this witness hostile to the Prosecution, because that would require open hostility to the Prosecution in his demeanour here. The witness, on the other hand, behaved very adequately towards the Prosecution and answered to the best his recollection and the best of his knowledge. First of all, it's absolutely inadmissible if the viva voce testimony does not suit the Prosecutor, then the witness statements that the Prosecution wrote themselves and to which the witness objects cannot be admitted into evidence. And the witness says that even Croat terms were used in these statements that the Prosecution tried to infiltrate here, and this shows how the Prosecution coaches the witnesses and then uses these arguments from previous decisions, written by the Prosecution themselves, to be admitted into evidence as an authentic statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate on the matter, decide whether this witness is hostile or not, which would entitle the Prosecution to put leading questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, as you could see, has deliberated on the matter and has acknowledged that the Prosecutor deems this witness is hostile. Therefore, the Prosecution is entitled to put leading questions to the witness. But as far as the admission of written statements is concerned, the Trial Chamber makes reservations and decides that this will be decided upon at a later stage. Therefore, at this stage, you may only put leading questions, and in the time allotted to you. I believe you still have an hour or so left. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And it was indeed my intention. I was just forecasting that I would be requesting the admission of the statement at a later stage. I was not intending to request it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a small piece of information the Trial Chamber would like to share with you. The Prosecutor has asked the Trial Chamber to declare that you are a hostile witness. The Trial Chamber has granted the application made by the Prosecution, which means that the Prosecution is entitled to put leading questions to you. Therefore, the situation is different to what it was before, and the Prosecution is entitled to put leading questions to you. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, just for your information, when you have been declared a hostile witness, it's a technical legal term. It doesn't mean that we think you in any way have acted inappropriately in court towards anyone here, just so you know that. Mr. Stojanovic, in 2004 you've already mentioned you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. I'd like to show you that statement, if the usher would assist me. And, Your Honours, the statement I'm showing is also in e-court as a new 65 ter number, 7265, and we could maybe call that up. Mr. Stojanovic, could I ask you to look at the first page of this statement, please.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Actually, if you would look at the front page, please. Could you go one page back? Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic, do you remember -- do you remember giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is your signature on the front page?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, what I would like you to do is to go with me through this statement. If you would now turn to the next page. Have you signed here on this page as well?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page, have you signed here?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would you turn once again to the page after this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. I just asked you whether your signature was on the page you're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would you now turn to the next page of your statement -- of the statement? Is your signature also on this page?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And on the next page of your statement -- or the statement, is your signature found there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if you would continue through, you turn it over again, is your signature on the page you're looking at? Maybe you would go through the statement.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we look at the last page of this, if you would stop -- if you would go back now to the page, Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the right-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner of the statement, there's a number. Actually, you're looking at the page now, I think. It is a page which, in the right-hand corner, has number 03603451. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And there have you signed a declaration?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And on what date did you sign the declaration?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here on the 18th of August, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you read out what that declaration says, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "This statement has been read over to me in the Serbian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily, and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So when you gave this statement, you knew that the statement might be used as evidence in criminal proceedings before this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you, therefore, took care to present the facts as precisely as you could when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And apart from the fact that there is some words in here which appear to be in Croatian, can you -- can you read this statement and understand it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I received this statement a month ago. This statement was read out to me from a laptop, where it was typed out. It wasn't taken out like this; that is to say, it was typed out on a laptop. And the statement that I signed, believing the OTP employee over there, the investigator, believing that what he read out to me was that, I signed it, and I did not receive a copy. This copy I received a month and a half ago, or perhaps even more than a month and a half ago. I was so astonished that many things are different from what was read out to me from the laptop; that is to say, it was typed out on the laptop by an investigator of the OTP in Belgrade, and the situation was quite different. Trusting Mr. Djuro, the investigator, I initialled all of these pages, but I did not receive the statement. I did not receive the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But on the 18th of August, 2004, you signed this very statement; right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely on the 18th of August, 2004, I read the statement. This statement was not read to me in the Serbian language. It was read out from the laptop, the computer, where it was signed. I waited for half an hour, an hour, for it to be printed out so that I could sign it, believing that gentleman of yours who put questions to me there; and it wasn't written that it would be used against Mr. Vojislav Seselj as an accused person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You've been a director of a company, I understand. Right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And as a director of a company, have you been signing business deals?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not sign it. I'm one of the directors. It is my superior who signs it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you ever signed any legal documents?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What, for example?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, something that my in-house lawyer would look at, or a lawyer; and I would sign it, trusting the man. I acted with full trust here, also, and that's why I reacted before coming into the courtroom. At the moment when I gave this statement, that can be read from the stenographic notes, that this statement was completely different. I stand by the fact that I signed this, but it is quite different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you can put your questions when it's time for your cross-examination. Let the Prosecutor do his job for the time being. He's trying to elicit from the witness the fact that he signed something, which he doesn't agree with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have the right to objections. If you are denying me that right, I'm not going to voice any objections anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are entitled to raise an objection if it is justified. For the time being, it is not justified. The Prosecutor is asking questions to see how it is that the witness has signed a statement that contains 42 paragraphs in his own language. This is what we're trying to find out. The witness has provided his explanation, which is worth what it's worth. Let the Prosecutor do his job. During the cross-examination, you can get back to this. Please proceed, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And today you are a financial manager. Is it also a custom for you, in your profession as a financial manager, to sign documents that you don't read?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to -- if the usher would collect that statement, please, and I'd like to show the witness another statement. Your Honours, this statement is in e-court as a new exhibit with 65 ter number 7264, and maybe we can call that document up. Mr. Stojanovic, would you look at the first page, please. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But I don't know the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. I've given you the wrong version. Could I get the usher to swap this. Well, we can leave the witness with the version that he has. Oh, okay. This is a translation of the document that I just showed you. Could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, again there was this interview. Paolo Pastore, Daniel Saxon, and Mr. Milan Kosanovic interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The only statement that is signed is the one in English, and the witness doesn't understand English. And the Serbian version is not signed. And it says in the witness acknowledgment, "The statement was read back to me in English." Obviously, the Prosecutor is trying to plant something on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but without you saying anything, the Trial Chamber has noticed this, that he signed the statement in English. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stojanovic, were you indeed interviewed in November 2004 by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and signed a statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And now I'd like to hand you back the copy that you had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, why did you sign the statement in English? Why didn't you sign the B/C/S version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they tell me that that is the correct version that I'm supposed to sign. I trust the investigators, and that's why I signed it. I don't know the English language. And in this courtroom, when I walked in, my first sentence here was that that text that I stated by way of a statement was quite different, and that is why I reacted, and that is why I said what can be read in the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do now, if I may, is just to let me know, is your signature on the front page of the statement that you're looking at now? I know it's in English, but is it your signature on the front page?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to go through the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have looked through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is your signature on all the pages of the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was just asked to initial these pages, not to write out my entire signature; just a little initial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you were interviewed by the OTP, if I'm putting questions to you it is because in the past I know what it is like to give statements - there was the investigator and an interpreter. The investigator was putting questions to you, and you answered the questions. Do we agree on this, Witness? Can we agree on this? The investigator puts a question to you in English; the interpreter translates the question, and you answer the question? Can we agree on this? This is how things happened? After that -- well, this lasted a while. The investigator has his laptop. He's going to write down your answers. Then he will give you a printout - that is why you had to wait for it - and then did the interpreter read the entire statement back to you, and then you signed the text in English, or did the interpreter not read it back to you? You trust the investigator and you sign the statement in English? Can you explain to us how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what happened: I came there, and we agreed that we should start working. I think it was afternoon. I remember that well, and the gentleman whose an investigator was typing on a laptop. He was typing in English, and I was speaking in Serbian, answering every question. So in relation to every one of these paragraphs, regardless of whether it was 8, 9, 10, whichever, then the interpreter would translate to me what was written by them over there. After we finished, then I was told to sign; that is to say, I did not have an opportunity to have the interpreter read the text back to me again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have paragraph 8 in front of us. You have it in English as well. Did the interpreter read paragraph 8 back to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what we have here is what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, because this is in English. I signed it at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. I understand. So the interpreter was telling you something, but since you don't speak English, you were not able to check. It would not have happened if things were done differently at the Tribunal, if, for instance, the statements were taken in the language of the witness and then the witness signs in his own language. The reason escapes me, actually, but this was the procedure that was adopted, so this is why you had to sign in English. But you may go on, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stojanovic, just to confirm, the statement was read back to you in your language, and then you signed the English copy of the statement and put your initials -- well, signed the first page, put your initials on the pages in the middle, and then you signed at the end; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was read out from the laptop. I'm telling you that again. I trusted the investigators, so what I signed in Serbian, I believed that that was it in English too. So I believe that if somebody gives an oath and says that what is shown to me -- I mean, what statement I gave, I believe that that is the way it would be written.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, it's quite complicated, it's complicated enough. You don't have to add on to this confusion. My questions were very clear. You don't have to add anything new. We've all understood how it was done, and during the cross-examination, if you wish to put more questions, even though the Judges understood very clearly, you may do so during your cross-examination. Mr. Marcussen, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like the usher to collect the statement and give the witness another statement, please. And, Your Honours, this statement is up-loaded into e-court as a new exhibit number, 7266 -- 65 ter number 7266.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- could you tell the Court what you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I have in front of me is some statement that I signed as well in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I seem to be making the same mistake again. Could we, with the assistance of the usher, swap the document? I think we should -- yeah, I think we should get the other one back, just to make sure we are looking at the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this document, what is this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a statement to. It says "witness information, witness statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what's the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 21st of June, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you recognise that statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise it because I see that I signed it. And I see my initials down there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what language is it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to go through that, as you did with the other ones, page by page --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I mean, I would like to ask you -- or, rather, tell you that this is in Croatian. This is not my language, Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to go through the statement and confirm that your initials are on each page?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough to look at page 16 -- well, the last page of the document you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 289 are the last digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is there -- sorry, on the page before this, is there an acknowledgment by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you read out that acknowledgment, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "This statement of 23 pages was read out to me in the Serbian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and I am aware it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 and I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." I signed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you would go to page 20 of the document that you have. If you would go back to page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what does the paragraph just above the signature read?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I confirm that I read the above paragraphs in my mother tongue and that the content is correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So on the 21st of June, 2006, you signed this statement, and you said that you had read the statement and that it was true, the truth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I've already said that all the statements that I received for signature -- well, in this sentence here, too -- I never would have signed -- well, first of all, it's not correct, I mean the Croatian words here "tocan" and all the rest. Well, it doesn't matter. It was read out to me from a laptop, and I waited for more than half an hour for all the documentation to be prepared so that I could sign it; that is to say, that I did not have enough time. And why would I think about this? Why would I not trust an investigator from The Hague if they gave me to initial something and said that that's what I gave them, why would I not believe that? The information contained in these statements, however, has been totally changed, because in the month of October -- I mean, that's why I brought my documentation. It says in October that I was at the frontline, and there is some information referred to as in May, June. This is a bit illogical. I cannot be somewhere where I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you're telling this Court that you are a man who has a Bachelor from a university, you hold various responsible positions in different companies, that you have given one statement to the OTP, to the Office of the Prosecutor, in 2004 which you signed without reading it; you gave a statement three months later in November about the same events, and that one was read back to you in English and you signed it, without knowing what you signed; and then you signed this particular statement and initialled every single page, and then put your signature on top of that at the last page just below a paragraph which said that you had read the statement? Do you want the Court to believe that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm telling you quite sincerely. You can check all of this. I did sign the statement, but as for what happened and the time distance, where I was at the time, that can be proven easily, very easily. There are organs and everything else, number 1. I said straight away, when I walked into this courtroom, this was my first objection addressed to the Trial Chamber and the president of the Trial Chamber. That is why I withdrew this documentation that you said I should not keep on the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you saw these documents again, you mentioned that it contained some things that you never said; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So consequently you believe that it was the investigator and the interpreter who made a mistake; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell untruth regarding some people. They read to me a completely different statement and I signed a completely different statement. I don't understand why something was read out to me from the laptop instead of printing it. I never received a single copy of what I signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the statement that we have before us, made on the 21st of June, 2007, if I take the first paragraph, randomly I take that paragraph, the interpreter must have read to you that first paragraph, even if you signed, or were you given the document and you read to yourself each page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I read this statement. I saw my name, I saw the personal details, and I initialled every page that was given me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did not check the content of the statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all, Judge, because I expected that the same statement will be given me to take home to analyse. That's the practice in our country and our courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you did sign the statements on the same day in which you gave your evidence, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, yes, but I had to wait a half hour or an hour for that to be printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had to wait an hour for it to be printed, and once it was printed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe more, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you signed right away; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was given me because Mr. Paolo was in a hurry to catch a plane and he said, "Hurry up, initial," because I usually don't just initial, I sign my full name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to observe -- could you see the printer or was the printer in the same room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not in the same room. I was on the ground floor of the UN building, the Prosecution office in Belgrade. I don't know where it was printed. There was a large desk, and the investigator behind the desk, sitting at a laptop. The interpreter was next to the investigator. I was on the other side of the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you together with Mr. Pastore-Stocchi and Mr. Saxon during the time that you waited for the printing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was with one man there, or maybe it was a woman, a girl. I can't remember. I had two coffees while waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understand you correctly, when you signed this statement for which you certify having heard and that the comments that are stated there are true and accurate, did you sign a false statement? Should I understand it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I did not review it. It was read back to me. I did not review the statement that I was signing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aside from the pages that you signed, at the very end of each page of each statement, you also certify that what you have said is true and that what you heard was true to fact. I mean, is that a false statement? That would be a false statement, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was led by the investigators on which page to sign, and that applied to the last page, including the witness acknowledgment. Why did the investigator ask me to sign my full name there, whereas I initialled all the rest? I was led, directed where to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I would just like to know one thing. At the very end, when you signed the last page, did anybody read out to you the two sentences that are written before -- above, rather, your signature: "I certify that ... ," so on and so forth. It's in Serbian. I can't remember the text exactly. Did anybody read that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even that was read back to me. I was just told, while we were writing the statement, number 1 was read to me, number 2 was read to me, as it was interpreted by the interpreter. And later, when it was printed out, that is, 60 minutes later - I remember it was quite a while - he took -- I was very warm, I was directed where to initial, where to put my initial. And on that last statement, the acknowledgment, the gentleman asked me to put my full signature. When I asked to get a copy, I was told that I cannot get a single copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, is Mr. Saxon here tonight?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I believe that he is, Your Honour. I don't know whether he's in the office today, but if your question is whether he works for the Office of the Prosecutor, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please ask him to come in right away, and then he can be sworn under oath and we will put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Would Your Honours -- should we have a short recess to get him down here, or how would we -- we can try to send him an e-mail and see if he's in the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, or the Registrar can call him and can ask him to come in immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe I may put some questions while we wait for that to be solved, or would Your Honours like us to wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, when you met the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor the first time in 2004, did you bring some documents with you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Am I correct there were two articles and three photographs?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you gave your statement in 2006, did you review that material again?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You did not?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you make comments on the material?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe we did make comments. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If you would go -- if you would go to -- in the statement you have with you, if you would go to the page which has number 0601-2286, please. It's nearly at the end. It's one of the last pages.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On this page, have you again put your signature on the page up towards the top?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what does the paragraph just above the signature say, if you would be kind enough to read it out?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I confirm that I read the above paragraphs in my mother tongue and the contents is truthful and correct." I have already stated, in regard to this and the other statements, that it was all read back to me from the computer, and I was waiting for all that to be printed out. Not for a moment did I hold a single statement in my hands to read all this myself or for the interpreter to read it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'd like now to talk about these statements with you and what is actually in the statements.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, could you just repeat to us again, were you a member of the SRS in -- no, sorry. You were, in fact, a member of the SRS in 2001, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 2001? I don't think so, unless they still keep me on the record of members. You mean 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I mean 1991. Thank you very much for your help. 1991.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was a member of the Serbian National Revival and the president of the District Board of the Serbian National Revival in Vranje. We had our own offices, we were an officially-registered party. We had an office received from the Municipality of Vranje and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you look at paragraph 8 of the statement you have in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry, but I need to clarify a point. Witness, you've told us that a month or a month and a half ago, you received those statements. Do you know who sent them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe even more. I believe it was in March, when we were writing the request, March or April, I said I wanted to be a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who gave you the statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My lawyer, who got in touch with the Defence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I am not mistaken, therefore, your lawyer received those statements from the Defence, if I understand correctly. Yes, very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Astounded me when I saw all the things that were written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, we're waiting for Mr. Saxon. I hope that he'll come shortly, because it's an order issued by the Trial Chamber, and it would be quite unpleasant, actually, if he did not show up. It is five minutes to 7.00. You are free to go, Witness. You will come back tomorrow. The hearing is starting at 9.00. The Witness and Victims Section will bring you to the Tribunal. Your examination-in-chief will continue tomorrow, and then Mr. Seselj will start his cross-examination. But, in any event, tomorrow we will end the proceedings at 1.45. And since you are now testifying, you cannot call the press, you cannot call the Prosecutor, you cannot call anybody, you cannot speak to Mr. Seselj's associates or anybody like that, but you can call your wife, your children. Of course, your family, you may speak to them, but you may not speak about this case with anyone. Did you understand me clearly? Very well.
